title: The beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7)
hookLine: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge"
carry: the first step through the door

cards: A grandmother's saying. A line taped above a desk. Something a coach shouted once that a player still repeats years later.
Short sayings travel. They fit in a pocket, and they come out at the right moment, often when the long explanation has been forgotten.

After Job, with its long speeches and its storm, the Writings turn to a whole book of these pocket sentences, one or two lines each. Easy to say, hard to live. Today's word is that book's Hebrew name.

teach.b: It's the Hebrew name of the book English calls Proverbs, taken from its opening words: the proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel.
Tradition links it to Solomon, the king remembered for asking God for wisdom. The book also names other voices further on, so it reads less like one lecture and more like a family's collected advice.
The opening verses say why it exists: to know wisdom, to understand words of insight, so the simple can grow shrewd and the young gain knowledge.

teach.h: THE FEAR OF THE LORD IS THE BEGINNING OF KNOWLEDGE.
teach.b: Then, before any advice, the line the whole book stands on: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge." Fear here is worth sitting with.

Some readers hear awe, the feeling of standing before something far bigger than yourself. Others hear a plainer fear: the care not to do wrong in God's sight, a respect that changes how a person acts.
Jewish teachers have read it more than one way. And notice the word beginning. Not the end of knowledge, as if faith replaces thinking.
Awe is where learning starts, the first step through the door, not a wall at the end of the hall. Job ended with God showing him stars and sea, and Job going quiet.
Mishlei starts from that quiet and builds a daily life on it: how to speak, how to work, how to treat a neighbor. Proverbs are small, but they assume something large behind them.

how: Mishlei is part of the Writings. Jews study it as practical wisdom for daily life, and its sayings are quoted at tables, in classrooms and in synagogue teaching.

practice: Take today's line, the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, or any verse from Proverbs you already know, and say it once slowly, then again with your eyes closed, then once more, letting each word land.
Keep it turning until you can say it without reaching for it. If you pray, you can let it be a prayer; if not, let it simply be yours.
